source.title_on_document: Can Gen AI Improve Creativity in Students with Low Academic Performance? A Quasi-Experimental Study Based on Chinese Samples

supplement.where: Appendices A-C are included in the saved publisher article text at https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/21582440261449529. No separate external supplement is referenced. There is no local PDF; in_this_pdf=false does not mean the appendices are missing from the source text.
supplement.holds: Appendix A, Table A1 describes intervention activities and teacher scaffolding; Appendix B, Table B1 and its worked example give creativity scoring rules; Appendix C, Table C1 gives Levene tests and degrees of freedom. Main-text Tables 2-3 contain creativity means, SDs, group Ns, ANOVA tests and partial eta squares; Results, Creativity Test Results gives robustness LMM F tests. No additional standard-error or confidence-interval tables are identified. Figures are absent from the saved export.

paper_design_summary: Three intact classes in a Shanghai secondary vocational school’s Innovation Training course were randomly assigned to traditional project-based instruction with web search, ChatGLM with minimal teacher intervention, or ChatGLM with teacher structure support (Methods, Intervention Design and Procedures; Appendix A, Table A1). The paper reports 75 selected students, but the sample headers and inferential statistics do not establish consistent analyzed counts (Methods, Participants; Tables 2-3; Appendix C, Table C1). Two researchers scored open-ended pre/post-test responses for fluency, originality, elaboration and flexibility; AI availability during the tests is unstated (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Procedures; Appendix B).

studies.label: Innovation Training: ChatGLM, teacher-supported ChatGLM, and traditional instruction

assignment.what_was_assigned: Three intact classes were randomly assigned to the three instructional conditions in their ordinary Innovation Training course. Each class received one condition; pre/post measurement was repeated within students, not within-person assignment to multiple AI conditions. This class-level allocation is distinct from the school administration’s earlier allocation of students to classes. Sequence generation and concealment are not described (Methods, Participants; Procedures, Phase I).
assignment.quote: Three entire classes were randomly assigned to the control group, experimental group 1, and experimental group 2.
assignment.locator: Methods, Procedures, Phase I (class assignment to conditions); Methods, Participants (prior allocation to classes); Discussion, Limitations and Conclusion (quasi-experimental label).

arms.name: EG1: ChatGLM with minimal teacher intervention
arms.description: Students used ChatGLM for autonomous exploration, brainstorming, SWOT analysis, surveys, marketing and entrepreneurial plans, and presentation language. The teacher intervened little (Methods, Intervention Design; Appendix A, Table A1). Reported sample N = 26 is printed in Methods, Participants and Table 2. The actual analyzed count is unresolved because Tables 2-3 inferential statistics and Appendix C, Table C1 conflict with the sample headers; n_analyzed is null. Assignment-stage people count is not separately given.

arms.name: EG2: ChatGLM with teacher structure support
arms.description: Students used ChatGLM with teacher support: clear task goals, task sheets, guiding questions, templates, process guidance and personalized feedback (Methods, Intervention Design; Appendix A, Table A1). Reported sample N = 22 is printed in Methods, Participants and Table 2. The actual analyzed count is unresolved because Tables 2-3 inferential statistics and Appendix C, Table C1 conflict with the sample headers; n_analyzed is null. Assignment-stage people count is not separately given.

arms.name: CG: traditional project-based instruction with web search available
arms.description: Teacher-led project-based instruction without ChatGLM, using lectures, cases, group brainstorming, textbooks, online materials and traditional tools. Students had access to web search tools such as Internet Explorer (Methods, Intervention Design and Procedures, Phase I; Appendix A, Table A1). Reported sample N = 27 is printed in Methods, Participants and Table 2. The actual analyzed count is unresolved because Tables 2-3 inferential statistics and Appendix C, Table C1 conflict with the sample headers; n_analyzed is null. Assignment-stage people count is not separately given.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions, attrition counts, outcome-specific complete-case counts, or missing-data rules are stated. Methods, Participants reports 75 students selected; Tables 2 and 4 print sample Ns of EG1 = 26, EG2 = 22 and CG = 27. These cannot be certified as analyzed counts: Appendix C, Table C1 prints df1 = 2 and df2 = 51 for all creativity Levene tests and df2 = 60 for psychological perceptions; the F and partial eta square values in Tables 2-4 corroborate inconsistent analysis denominators (see notes for conditional arithmetic checks). Study and arm n_analyzed fields are null; printed sample Ns are retained only with an explicit qualification. No alternative analyzed counts or numbers of excluded people are entered as confirmed facts. Appendix B removes inappropriate or irrelevant responses, without reporting participant exclusions. Separate counts at assignment are not given, so n_randomized remains null.
participants.who: 11th-grade students aged 16 to 17 in the same Engineering major at a secondary vocational school in Shanghai. The three intact classes followed the same curriculum with the same teacher; the population is described as having low academic performance in the Chinese vocational education context (Methods, Participants).
participants.quote: A total of 75 11th-grade students from 3 intact classes in a secondary vocational school in Shanghai were selected for this study.
participants.locator: Methods, Participants and Data analysis; Results, Tables 2-4; Appendix B, coding procedure; Appendix C, Table C1.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGLM; specific model version not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Students used the conversational assistant during project-based learning for idea generation, SWOT analysis, surveys, marketing and entrepreneurial plans, and presentation language; EG2 added teacher structure support. The tool is described as based on a model trained by Zhipu AI Company and Tsinghua University KEG Lab (Methods, Intervention Design; Appendix A, Table A1). The interface figure is absent and no exact model version is stated.

task.description: The scored outputs are open-ended divergent-thinking test responses, not the classroom business plans. Pre-test: innovative strategies to make daily life more convenient. Post-test: innovative strategies to build an international child-friendly city in Shanghai. Tests draw on four ATTA dimensions without using its original questions. Training involves a business-plan project (Methods, Intervention Design and Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Appendices A-B).
task.duration: Each test: 15 minutes. Study: 12 weeks, comprising preparation/pre-test (2 weeks), intervention (9 weeks, 90 minutes per week), and post-test (1 week) (Methods, Procedures and Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity).

outcomes.name: Ability of fluency
outcomes.measure_detail: Two researchers scored pre/post-test responses, with agreement coefficients all higher than 0.76 (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity). Appendix B describes two trained independent raters and verification/discussion of coding. Scores are manually coded counts per participant. Fluency counts distinct, relevant, non-repetitive ideas, with one point per valid idea; irrelevant or repeated responses are excluded (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Appendix B, Table B1). Table 2 omnibus time × group interaction: F = 7.274, p = .002, partial η² = 0.222. Results, Creativity Test Results reports a robustness linear mixed-effects model with class as a random factor: F = 5.895, p < .01. This is a variant of the same outcome; no pairwise class-adjusted coefficients, standard errors or confidence intervals are provided. The contrast concerns pre/post trajectories on different test scenarios. Test-time AI access and immediate versus delayed session timing cannot be confirmed; question, ai_available_when_produced and timing are null (Methods, Procedures; Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity). Table 2 sample Ns are printed values, not verified analyzed counts; study and arm n_analyzed fields are null because the inferential statistics and Appendix C degrees of freedom conflict with those headers. See participants.exclusions and notes.
outcomes.delay: Phase III is a 1-week post-test phase following the 9-week Phase II intervention. This is a phase duration, not a stated delay after the final intervention session or last AI use. Whether testing was in the same session or a later session, and the exact interval in days, are not explicit (Methods, Procedures, Phases II-III).

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met: Methods, Procedures, Phase I explicitly says the three intact classes were randomly assigned to the instructional conditions; ChatGLM supplied generative-AI assistance during creative project work (Intervention Design; Appendix A, Table A1). Criterion 2 is met at the 50-person threshold, although the exact analyzed total and arm counts remain unresolved: Methods, Participants reports 75 selected students and Table 2 prints sample Ns of 26, 22 and 27, whereas the creativity degrees of freedom in Appendix C, Table C1 and the statistics in Tables 2-3 are consistent with 54 analyzed people under the stated standard ANOVA model. The latter is a conditional arithmetic diagnostic, not a source-reported replacement count; both alternatives exceed 50. Accordingly, structured analyzed counts are null while the threshold decision remains met. Criterion 3 is met because two researchers scored student-produced open-ended responses (Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Appendix B, Table B1). Unstated test-time AI availability leaves with_ai versus after_ai unresolved but does not negate any of these three criteria. The authors’ quasi-experimental label does not override their explicit class-randomization statement. Screening eligibility does not establish adequate precision for pooling.

one_line_finding: Teacher-supported ChatGLM showed larger pre/post gains than control in fluency, originality, elaboration and flexibility (Table 3: p = .001, .001, <.001 and .004), while ChatGLM alone showed no clear advantage; exact analyzed counts and test-time AI availability remain unresolved (Tables 2-3; Appendix C, Table C1; Methods, Procedures).
open_questions: Was ChatGLM available while students produced responses during either creativity test, especially the post-test? Methods, Procedures and Measurements do not state that AI was removed or permitted. All four question and ai_available_when_produced fields remain null; neither with_ai nor after_ai is confirmed.

Was the post-test in the same session as the final intervention activity or a later session, and how long after the last AI use? The 1-week Phase III is not an explicit test delay. Immediate versus delayed timing remains unresolved for S1-O1, S1-O2, S1-O3 and S1-O4 (Methods, Procedures, Phases II-III).

What were the actual analyzed counts by arm and outcome, and were any people excluded or lost? Methods, Participants reports 75 selected students and Tables 2/4 print sample Ns of 26, 22 and 27; Appendix C, Table C1 gives creativity df1 = 2, df2 = 51 and psychological-perception df2 = 60. The F and partial eta square values in Tables 2-4 corroborate conflicting analysis denominators. The conditional arithmetic checks in notes are not source-reported counts, so study and arm n_analyzed fields remain null pending authors’ complete-case counts and an explanation or correction of the tables.

What allocation procedure randomized the three classes? Phase I explicitly reports class randomization, while the title and Limitations call the study quasi-experimental; sequence generation and concealment are unspecified (Methods, Procedures; Discussion, Limitations and Conclusion).

Are class-adjusted pairwise estimates and uncertainty available? The source gives omnibus LMM F tests with class as a random factor, but no pairwise coefficients, standard errors or confidence intervals; only three classes were assigned (Results, Creativity Test Results).

Which operational scoring rules were applied? Originality uses less than 5% in Methods, no more than 5% of participants in Table B1, and the worked example refers to ≤3 participants with a parenthetical about total ideas. Elaboration counts detailed responses in Methods/the example and detail instances in Table B1. Flexibility categories are pre-generated in Methods but determined during coding in Appendix B.

The saved publisher text lacks figure graphics, including Figures 2 and 4; those images could contain additional information about the ChatGLM configuration or testing procedure. No local PDF is provided (retrieval.json, c044.text_only_note; saved source header).
notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09 after reading the entire 934-line publisher article text, including Appendices A-C, references and metadata, and all three challenge files. retrieval.json has pdf_path=null; the saved publisher text is the source of record and section/table locators replace page numbers. No PDF, web search or external API was used; absent figure graphics were not reconstructed. All four output-scored outcomes and twelve pairwise contrasts were retained. Their printed means, SDs, sample headers, F tests, p values and partial eta squares were checked against Tables 2-3; the class-random-factor LMM F tests were checked against Results, Creativity Test Results. No effect sizes or standard errors were computed. Two people-count challenges were corrected by replacing the analyzed total and all analyzed arm counts with null and qualifying the printed sample Ns. The outcome challenge remains open because the source does not state test-time AI access. Conditional count audit only: for standard ANOVA, df_error = df_effect * F * (1 - partial_eta_squared) / partial_eta_squared. Allowing each printed F and partial eta square its three-decimal rounding interval, every Table 2 creativity outcome permits only integer df_error = 51 with df_effect = 2; every Table 3 creativity outcome permits only 32, 39 and 31 for EG1 versus CG, EG2 versus CG and EG1 versus EG2, respectively, with df_effect = 1. Appendix C independently prints creativity df1 = 2 and df2 = 51 in all eight pre/post rows. If these statistics are correct for the stated three-group analysis, N = df_error + 3 = 54. For pairwise analyses, N = df_error + 2 gives conditional pair totals of 34, 41 and 33. If the same cases from each arm were used in every pairwise comparison, EG1 = (34 + 33 - 41) / 2 = 13, EG2 = (41 + 33 - 34) / 2 = 20, and CG = (34 + 41 - 33) / 2 = 21. These calculations confirm the checker’s discrepancy; none is an author-confirmed participant count, and none is entered into a structured N field.
